turns.input: $crumb I built the little bucket-return tracker in this folder for independent Toronto event florists. I have zero users and no florist contacts. I want to find out whether this deserves another weekend before adding anything. Help me get the first useful conversations ready. Do not build or contact anyone.
turns.output:
The tracker is enough to start learning. The next weekend has to earn its place through florists’ actual return headaches. I’ll look at what you’ve built and prepare a small conversation pack with reachable Toronto starting points, without building or contacting anyone.

There’s a useful wrinkle: local florists already offer teardown and pickup, so “things need returning” doesn’t yet prove they need a tracker. We need to find out whether buckets actually stay behind, who chases them, and whether that costs enough to matter. I’m shaping the conversations around their last event, before showing the app.

The conversation pack is ready, including four public starting points and a counterexample worth hearing from. The key distinction is buckets versus rental décor: a florist can have plenty of rental inventory and still have no bucket-return problem. The decision rule now requires concrete bucket incidents, rather than enthusiasm for the idea.

**Hold the next build weekend.** The missing evidence is whether florists repeatedly spend meaningful time or money recovering buckets—and whether their existing workaround fails.

I prepared the [conversation pack](<USER>/AppData/Local/Temp/crumb-closeout-0zIUwL/independent-existing/discovery/FIRST_CONVERSATIONS.md) and [lead sheet](<USER>/AppData/Local/Temp/crumb-closeout-0zIUwL/independent-existing/discovery/LEADS.csv). No product changes or contact with anyone.

Start with the owner/operator who handles equipment recovery and sometimes leaves buckets at venues. Four public starting points:

| Starting point | Why it’s useful |
|---|---|
| [Neroli](https://www.nerolidesign.com/weddings) | Lists rental items and teardown. Bucket practices remain unknown. |
| [Token Blooms](https://www.tokenblooms.ca/) | Vaughan-based, serves Toronto; rentals and an existing client portal. Useful for learning what already works. |
| [Sweetpea’s](https://sweetpeaevents.ca/contact/) | Toronto event-floral studio. Weaker fit until bucket practices are confirmed; closed to public visits. |
| [Posy](https://www.posyevents.ca/faq) | Counterexample: **24-hour rentals with company-managed returns** may leave little overdue-return problem. |

Their public contact routes are in the sheet. None has expressed interest; independence and bucket workflow need confirming.

The invitation is ready to personalize:

> Hi [studio team], I noticed [verified detail]. I’m trying to understand how independent event florists handle reusable equipment after an event. I made a small bucket-return prototype, but I’m checking whether the problem matters before spending more time on it.
>
> Would the person who handles pack-out and returns be open to a 15-minute conversation about your last event? There’s no demo or purchase request. If this isn’t relevant, no need to reply.

Keep the app out of the first conversation. Ask:

1. What’s the hardest part of wrapping up an event and getting reusable equipment back?
2. Tell me about the last time you encountered that.
3. Why was it difficult?
4. What have you tried to handle it?
5. What do you dislike about those solutions—and what works well?

Then pin down whether **buckets** were involved, who chased them, actual messages/trips/time, replacement costs, and frequency. Rental-vase trouble isn’t automatically bucket trouble.

**My proposed hurdle:** three qualified conversations by October 13. Another bounded test is earned if two independently describe recent, costly bucket-return incidents with inadequate workarounds, and one agrees to walk through a real upcoming return task. If recovery is routine or already handled well, park it. Silence means recruitment is unresolved.

Compliments won’t earn the weekend. A concrete story about the chase might.
